# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 33 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 33 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_033_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 5, Chapter 1 — Patience and Anger

**1** "Be patient and long-suffering," he said, "and you will have mastery over all wickedness and will practice all righteousness. **2** For if you are patient, the Holy Spirit who dwells in you will remain pure, undarkened by any other evil spirit; he will dwell in a spacious place, rejoicing, and together with the vessel in which he dwells he will serve the Lord with great cheerfulness, having peace within himself. **3** But whenever an angry spirit enters, the Holy Spirit — being tender — immediately feels confined and finds no clean place; he seeks to depart. For the angry spirit chokes him, leaving him no room to serve the Lord as he wishes, being polluted by the angry spirit. For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger. **4** When both spirits inhabit the same place — the moment the spirit of anger enters — the Holy Spirit is grieved and that person is left without him. **5** The spirit of patience is dear to God and acceptable to him, and in patience the Lord dwells. The spirit of anger, however, is unprofitable and destroys the person in whom it dwells."

---

### Council Notes

Mandate 5.1 introduces the Shepherd's pneumatological ethics. The framework is striking: moral virtues and vices are not simply habits of the will but *spirits* that inhabit the person and affect the indwelling Holy Spirit.

The description of the Holy Spirit as "tender" (hapalos) is unique in early Christian literature. The Spirit is not presented as an overwhelming divine power but as a sensitive, relational presence that responds to the spiritual climate of the person.

The cosmological dualism — "the Lord dwells in patience; the devil dwells in anger" — is not ontological dualism (equal forces) but a moral map: each virtue/vice has a divine or demonic correlate.

The practical implication: anger is not merely a character flaw but a spiritual displacement activity — it drives out the Holy Spirit and invites demonic presence. This is a serious warning, consistent with Ephesians 4:26-27: "Do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil."
